passage: Monday: Siddharth, two, curled his fingers back and forth at Manoj, eyes on the biscuit tin he couldn't open. Manoj came over and opened it. Tuesday: Manoj offered a woolly hat and Siddharth pushed his palm out flat, turning his face away. Manoj put the hat down. Wednesday: Siddharth pushed his palm at the plate of peas, but a second later curled his fingers towards Manoj's chair, looking at his father's face. Manoj laughed and sat beside him.

qa.q: What did Siddharth want opened on Monday?
qa.a: The biscuit tin.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling each time he moved his hand, and how can you tell?
qa.a: With the curled fingers he was eager for help with the tin, and with the flat palm he was unwilling to take the hat or the peas, since he turned his face away. On Wednesday he seemed happy to have his father close, beckoning him to sit beside him.

qa.q: What could Manoj do to build on these signals?
qa.a: He could say the words that match each gesture, such as “come” and “no thank you”, and respond quickly.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel when Siddharth pushes the hat away?
qa.a: He may feel a little unheard at first, but noticing the gesture as communication helps him accept it. 🙂

grounding: A toddler beckons with a curled hand and pushes a hand outward to refuse, and the meaning depends on what the child is looking at.

passage: On the balcony of their flat, Vishal, two, crouched over a snail on the rim of a flower pot. He looked up at his mother Usha and curled his hand towards himself, again and again. “Come see?” said Usha. She knelt beside him. Then she held out her phone to take a picture and Vishal pushed his hand out flat towards it, lips pressed. She put the phone down. “Okay, no phone.” He tapped the pot with one finger, looking at the snail.

qa.q: Where did Vishal find the snail?
qa.a: On the rim of a flower pot on the balcony.

qa.q: What does Vishal want with each of his hand movements?
qa.a: The curled hand asked Usha to come and see the snail, and the pushed hand told her to keep the phone away. He might have worried the phone would disturb the snail.

qa.q: What could Usha try next?
qa.a: She could keep the phone away, sit quietly and watch the snail with Vishal and use words like “slow snail”.

qa.q: How might Usha feel when Vishal pushes his hand at the phone?
qa.a: Usha may be a little surprised, but she respects his wish, since she puts the phone down and says, “Okay, no phone.”

grounding: A toddler beckons with a curled hand to invite a parent and pushes a hand outward to refuse, with meaning depending on his focus.

passage:
"Look, Kalyani, she's calling you." Vasudha, in her high chair, was curling all her fingers toward her mother.
Kalyani came over. "Yes, baby?"
Vasudha looked down at the bowl of bitter gourd and pushed her flat hand out at it, hard.
"Is she waving bye to me now?" asked Grandpa.
"No, look where she's looking. That hand is for the karela."
Kalyani moved the bowl away. Vasudha curled her fingers again, at the bread basket.

qa.q: What was in the bowl Vasudha pushed her hand at?
qa.a: Bitter gourd, called karela.

qa.q: What did Vasudha's two hand gestures show she wanted?
qa.a: The curled fingers showed she wanted her mother close, and later the bread; the pushing hand showed dislike of the bitter gourd and a wish to send it away.

qa.q: How did Kalyani work out what the pushing hand meant?
qa.a: She looked at where Vasudha was looking, at the bowl, instead of guessing from the gesture alone.

qa.q: How does Grandpa read the pushing hand at first?
qa.a: Grandpa thinks it might be a wave goodbye to Kalyani, not noticing it was aimed at the food.

grounding: A toddler beckons her mother and pushes her hand out at food she dislikes, the meaning shown by where she looks.

passage: Daycare note, Thursday. At circle time, when another child brought the drum right up to Raghav's face, he pushed his hand out flat toward it and turned his head away. I moved the drum back and he settled. Later in the block corner he caught my eye and curled his fingers at me, over and over, until I came. He wanted me to see his tower. The same small hands meant "go away" and "come here" within an hour. Sunaina, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Raghav want Sunaina to see?
qa.a: His tower in the block corner.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he pushed his hand out at the drum?
qa.a: He likely felt overwhelmed or annoyed by the drum so close to his face and wanted it away; later his beckoning showed pride and a wish to share his tower.

qa.q: Which choice of Sunaina's worked, and why?
qa.a: Moving the drum back worked, because it respected his "go away" gesture and he settled quickly.

qa.q: How might the child with the drum see Raghav's pushing hand?
qa.a: The child might feel rejected or confused, having meant to share the drum.

grounding: A teacher reads a toddler's outward push as protest and his curled fingers as invitation, depending on what he is looking at.

passage:
In the courtyard of their small-town house after the rain, Nikita squatted by a puddle and curled her fingers hard toward the verandah. "Papa! Papa!"
Anand came out. There, by the puddle, sat a fat green frog.
Anand crouched beside her. The frog hopped, landing close to her toes. Nikita jerked back and pushed both flat hands out at it. "No! No!"
Anand laughed softly and lifted her up. "Too close. Let's watch from here."

qa.q: What was sitting by the puddle?
qa.a: A fat green frog.

qa.q: What changed in Nikita's feelings between the two gestures?
qa.a: First she was excited and curious and beckoned her father to share the frog; when it hopped close, she was startled and a little scared, pushing her hands out to send it away.

qa.q: What did Anand do well when the frog hopped close?
qa.a: He lifted her away and suggested watching from a distance, respecting her "go away" push.

qa.q: How might Anand feel being called out to see the frog?
qa.a: He probably feels pleased and included that Nikita wanted to share her discovery with him.

grounding: A toddler beckons her father to see a frog and pushes her hands out when it hops close, meaning shifting with what she sees.

passage:
In a Berlin playground, Elif squatted by the wet sandpit. She looked back at her mother, Soo-ah, and curled her small hand towards herself, again and again.
Soo-ah came over. Elif pointed at a snail on the edge.
“Oh! A snail!”
Later Soo-ah held out a sunhat. Elif pushed her hand out flat against it, turned away and frowned.
“No hat? Okay, we'll sit in the shade.”

qa.q: What did Elif point at in the sandpit?
qa.a: She pointed at a snail on the edge.

qa.q: What did Elif want when she curled her hand towards herself, and when she pushed her hand out?
qa.a: The curling hand was an invitation: she was excited and wanted Soo-ah to come and see the snail. The flat push showed protest; she was annoyed and wanted the hat taken away.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah read Elif's gestures well?
qa.a: She looked at what Elif was looking at each time, the snail and then the hat, so she understood the invitation and the refusal.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel when Elif waves her over to the snail?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and included, since Elif wanted to share her discovery with her.

grounding: It shows a toddler beckoning with a curled hand to call a parent and pushing a hand outward to refuse, with meaning read from what she is looking at.
